Adult Cervical Spine Deformity
 CORE
September 15, 2022

Highlight
Show highlights
FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Define adult cervical spine deformity and the associated radiographic parameters.
Identify the underlying pathologic processes that may contribute to cervical spine deformity.
Recognize the imaging modalities used to assess cervical spine deformity.
Review the surgical management of cervical spine deformity.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Adult cervical spine deformity is malalignment of the cervical spine that may pathologically
alter posture and may be associated with considerable pain, neurologic injury, and disability.
Causes of primary cervical deformity include degenerative changes, inflammatory conditions,
noninflammatory myopathy, iatrogenic causes, and trauma.

Secondary cervical deformity may result from concurrent thoracolumbar spine deformity or in
response to surgical correction of such deformity.
Anatomy and Biomechanics

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The cervical spine has an important role in the normal physiologic position and function
of the head and neck. It carries the weight of the cranium; protects vital neurovascular
structures, including the spinal cord, nerve roots, and vertebral arteries; and has the
largest range of motion of the regions of the spine. The physiologic range of motion of
the cervical spine consists of approximately 90° of flexion, 70° of extension, up to 45° of
lateral bending, and up to 90° of bilateral rotation.1
The atlantooccipital joint allows for flexion and extension, and the atlantoaxial joints are
primarily responsible for lateral rotation of the cervical spine. The flexible nature of the
cervical spine enables compensation for changes in the distal spine, which allows for
maintenance of horizontal gaze. The cervical spine is susceptible to acute injury and
chronic disease processes because of this inherent flexibility.
Normal Cervical Alignment
The radiographic parameters commonly used to assess cervical spine alignment include the
following:
Cervical lordosis
C2 through C7 sagittal vertical axis (cSVA)
Chin-brow vertical angle (CBVA)
T1 slope (T1S)

Normal Cervical Alignment
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:10 AM
AAOS | Adult Cervical Spine Deformity
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004088
2/19

Cervical lordosis may be measured via various different methods, including the modified
Cobb method, Jackson physiologic stress lines, Harrison posterior tangent method, and
the Ishihara index2 (Figure 1). Cervical lordosis may be altered with posture and changes
in thoracic kyphosis. With normal aging, increased thoracic kyphosis and decreased
lumbar lordosis frequently are compensated by increased cervical lordosis to maintain
horizontal gaze. The angle of cervical lordosis is reported as a negative value, and the
angle of kyphosis is reported as a positive value. Controversy exists with regard to the
normal range of cervical lordosis, with some studies reporting a mean of 35° to 40° in
asymptomatic patients,3 and other studies noting that non-lordotic cervical spinal
alignment is normal in as much as one-third of the population.4 In general, cervical
lordosis of −10° (ie, a cervical kyphosis of 10°) indicates spinal deformity.
Figure 1 Lateral radiographs of a cervical spine demonstrate common techniques for
measuring cervical lordosis. A, Modified Cobb method. B, Jackson physiologic stress
lines. C, Harrison posterior tangent method. D, Ishihara index. (Reproduced with
permission from Tan LA, Riew KD, Traynelis VC: Cervical spine deformity: Part 1.
Biomechanics, radiographic parameters, and classification. Neurosurgery 2017;81[2]:197-
203.)
cSVA is a measure of regional sagittal alignment, calculated as the distance between
plumb lines drawn from C2 and C7. cSVA is a measure of the relationship between C2
and C7 in the sagittal plane. A cSVA greater than 50 mm is considered a deformity
threshold.5
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:10 AM
AAOS | Adult Cervical Spine Deformity
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004088
3/19

The CBVA is an indirect measure of horizontal gaze, calculated as the angle formed at
the intersection of a vertical line and a line between the chin and the brow. If the head is
tilted down, CBVA has a positive value; if the head is tilted up, CBVA is a negative value. A
value of 0° indicates a neutral position. The estimated normal range is −10° to 20°.
The T1S is the angle formed by the upper endplate of the T1 vertebra and the horizontal
plane, comparable to sacral slope in the lumbar spine. The T1S correlates with thoracic
kyphosis and global malalignment. The difference between The T1S and C2 through C7
cervical lordosis has been proposed to assess cervical alignment, similar to assessment
of pelvic incidence-lumbar lordosis mismatch of the lumbar spine and pelvis.6 A T1S–
cervical lordosis of less than 20° is considered normal.
Natural History

Natural History
The structural changes that may result in symptomatic cervical deformity include
scoliosis, kyphosis, hyperlordosis, spondylolisthesis, and retrolisthesis. The most
prevalent form of cervical deformity is cervical kyphosis.
Patients often report neck pain initially but also may have associated myelopathy and
sensorimotor deficits secondary to neural element compression. With marked cervical
kyphosis, dysphagia and difficulty maintaining horizontal gaze may occur.
Etiology
Degenerative Changes

Degenerative Changes
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:10 AM
AAOS | Adult Cervical Spine Deformity
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004088
4/19

Degenerative changes of the cervical spine commonly involve disk degeneration with
bulging of the intervertebral disks and osteophyte formation, which narrows the spinal
canal and foramen. These changes result in a spectrum of disorders, ranging from
patients who are asymptomatic to patients with neck pain, stiffness, or injury to the
spinal cord and nerve roots (Resource 1). Approximately 60% of the population will
experience some form of cervical spine degenerative change in their lifetime.7 Patients
with severe degenerative changes may have deformity, most commonly cervical
kyphosis, and cervical myelopathy that results from spinal cord compression and/or
tension.
Inflammatory Arthritides

Inflammatory Arthritides
Inflammatory arthritides include seronegative spondyloarthropathies and rheumatoid
arthritis. Typically, rheumatoid arthritis is found in the upper cervical spine, with cervical
spine involvement in an estimated 80% of patients.8 This may manifest as atlantoaxial
subluxation or subaxial subluxation in severe cases. If subluxation affects multiple levels
of the cervical spine, a staircase deformity may be observed (Figure 2).
Ankylosing spondylitis, the most common seronegative spondyloarthropathy, also may
affect the cervical spine. Ankylosing spondylitis leads to contracture and fusion of the
cervical spine, with subsequent kyphosis and risk of three-column fracture.9

Figure 2 Lateral radiograph of the cervical spine of a patient with rheumatoid arthritis
demonstrates a characteristic staircase deformity. (Reproduced from Allen RT, Upsani
VV: Inflammatory arthritides of the spine, in Rao RD, Smuck M, eds: Orthopaedic
Knowledge Update: Spine, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2012, pp 549-563.)
Dropped Head Syndrome

Dropped Head Syndrome
Dropped head syndrome often results from neuromuscular disease, and patients
present with a characteristic cervical kyphosis that causes the chin to drop to the chest
(Figure 3). If dropped head syndrome is the result of kyphosis, the deformity often is
flexible and associated with extensor muscle atrophy in the cervical spine. Changes in
bony architecture also may occur secondary to local inflammatory processes.10 This rare
pathology is noteworthy for its severity.

Figure 3 Clinical photograph shows a woman who is standing and has weakness of the
posterior neck musculature that resulted in a chin-on-chest deformity. (Reproduced
from Sharan AD, Kaye D, Charles Malveaux WM, Riew KD: Dropped head syndrome:
Etiology and management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2012;20[12]:766-774.)
Adult Spine Deformity

Adult Spine Deformity
Patients with secondary cervical deformities may have concomitant pathology in the
thoracic, lumbar, or sacropelvic spine. Cervical kyphosis may develop in patients with
adult spine deformity to maintain horizontal gaze. Some studies have shown that as
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:10 AM
AAOS | Adult Cervical Spine Deformity
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004088
7/19

many as 53% of patients with thoracolumbar deformity have a cervical spine
deformity.11
Deformity in the cervical spine also may result from a reciprocal change after adult spine
deformity surgery. A major complication of surgical adult spine deformity correction is
proximal junctional kyphosis, which is defined as an increase of more than 10° in the
upper instrumented vertebra. Long-standing proximal junctional kyphosis may cause
structural changes in the cervical spine because of sustained anterior column
compression.
Classification
Currently no universally accepted classification system exists for cervical spine deformities.
Ames Criteria
Ames et al12 proposed a classification system for cervical deformity. This classification system
consists of a primary driver of deformity and five modifiers. The primary drivers, which are
based on the apex of the deformity, include the following:
Cervical
Cervicothoracic
Thoracic
Coronal
Craniovertebral junction
The modifiers are as follows:
cSVA
CBVA
Mismatch of T1S and cervical lordosis
Modified Japanese Orthopedic Association score
Scoliosis Research Society–Schwab classification of thoracolumbar deformity


Patient History and Physical Examination
Key components in the assessment of cervical deformity are evaluation of flexibility,
neurological deficit, swallowing difficulty, and quality of life (Figure 4). Neurologic
evaluation may guide surgical management because it helps determine the need for
neural element decompression.
Figure 4 Clinical photograph shows a patient whose head is completely suspended in air
because of rigid cervical kyphosis (head suspension test). (Reproduced from Cho SK,
Safir S, Lombardi JM, Kim JS: Cervical spine deformity: Indications, considerations, and
surgical outcomes. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2019;27[12]:e555-e567.)
Imaging Studies
Radiography


Radiography
Full-body imaging studies are essential because global spine alignment relies on
compensatory mechanisms involving the spine, pelvis, and lower extremities. Full-length
standing radiographs are obtained to assess the following:
Location of the deformity
Spinal balance
Concurrent thoracolumbar deformity
Flexion-extension, traction, and supine radiographs allow for assessment of flexibility.
Computed Tomography

Computed Tomography
CT is an important component of preoperative imaging because it helps identify optimal
fixation points for the fusion construct and assessment of fused segments. In patients
with a stiff cervical spine deformity because of ankylosis or congenital abnormalities, CT
may be used to guide osteotomies during surgical correction. CT angiography may be
valuable before surgical deformity correction via a planned anterior approach to confirm
carotid and vertebral artery anatomy. Kissing carotids are common in patients with
cervical kyphosis. The vertebral artery enters the foramen transversarium at C6 in 90%
of patients; therefore, confirmation of the course is necessary.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:10 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004088
10/19

MRI aids in assessment of neurologic compression and guides surgical planning by
helping the surgeon determine the optimal proximal and distal ends of the fusion
construct (Figure 5). Given that MRI generally is performed with the patient in a relaxed
supine position, this imaging modality also helps to indicate the flexibility of the
deformity. In addition, MRI can identify fatty infiltration in the muscle envelope, which is
a poor prognostic factor for junctional failure and undesirable reciprocal changes.
Figure 5 Images of the cervical spine of an adult patient with Klippel-Feil syndrome.
Preoperative AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs demonstrate kyphoscoliosis. C, Sagittal
MRI shows stenosis. AP (D) and lateral (E) radiographs obtained after C2 through T3
circumferential reconstruction. (Reproduced from Cho SK, Safir S, Lombardi JM, Kim JS:
Cervical spine deformity: Indications, considerations, and surgical outcomes. J Am Acad
Orthop Surg 2019;27[12]:e555-e567.)

Surgical Management
Indications

Indications
Surgical treatment is reserved for symptomatic patients. The goals of surgical
management include restoration of ideal sagittal and/or coronal malalignment,
decompression of neural elements, and restoration of horizontal gaze. Surgical
management of cervical spine deformity is technically complex, and preferred
approaches vary among experts; however, considerable potential exists for clinical
improvement in select populations.
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
Preoperative planning should include radiographic evaluation of global and cervical spine
alignment, identification of a primary driver, and assessment of neurologic deficits.
Tan et al13 proposed seven factors that should be consider before management of a cervical
spine deformity.
Presence of neurologic compression
Flexibility of the deformity
Presence of ankylosis
Location of the deformity
Previous surgical management
Presence of degenerative changes at proximal/distal vertebral levels
General medical status
Surgical Approaches

Surgical Approaches
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:10 AM
AAOS | Adult Cervical Spine Deformity
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004088

The surgical techniques to correct cervical spine deformity vary and depend on the
pathology (Resource 1). Surgical approaches include anterior-only, posterior-only, and
combined anteroposterior or posterior-anteroposterior approaches. Specific techniques
include anterior cervical diskectomy and fusion (ACDF), cervical corpectomy, Smith-
Petersen osteotomy, and pedicle subtraction osteotomy, all of which may be combined
to optimize outcomes (Figure 6).
Figure 6 Lateral radiographs of the spine of a patient with rigid cervical kyphosis after
laminectomy and fusion (A); the patient underwent C2 through T4 revision fusion with a
T2 pedicle subtraction osteotomy to correct the deformity while avoiding C8 or T1
radiculopathy (B). (Reproduced from Cho SK, Safir S, Lombardi JM, Kim JS: Cervical spine
deformity: Indications, considerations, and surgical outcomes. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2019;27[12]:e555-e567.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:10 AM
AAOS | Adult Cervical Spine Deformity
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004088
13/19

In general, decompression may be performed anteriorly or posteriorly based on spinal
pathology and indications. An anterior approach is beneficial if instability or deformity
(shortening) of the anterior column is present.
Osteotomies are reserved to correct severe kyphotic deformities. Common anterior
techniques used to improve cervical lordosis include ACDF, anterior corpectomy, and
anterior osteotomy. In general, ACDF at a single level may result in 3° to 5° of lordosis, a
Smith-Petersen osteotomy may result in approximately10° of lordosis, an anterior
osteotomy may result in approximately 17° of lordosis, and a pedicle subtraction
osteotomy may result in as much as 35° of lordosis. Posterior-based three-column
osteotomies are performed most often at T2 or below to minimize the risk of vertebral
artery injury; however, they may be performed as superiorly as C7 given that the vessel
typically does not pass through the C7 transverse foramen. Correction via osteotomy is
maintained with the use of a fusion construct.
The posterior approach can be used in patients with pronounced cervical lordosis
because this deformity does not require anterior column lengthening to restore normal
gaze. In addition, in patients with a flexible cervical spine deformity or patients in whom
a deformity is reducible via traction, correction may be accomplished via an isolated
posterior approach with decompression and instrumented fusion.
A combined approach, either as a same-day or staged procedure, may be considered if
one approach is deemed insufficient. This may occur in patients with severe rigid cervical
kyphosis or ventral compression or in patients with compromised ventral column
integrity. A combined approach predisposes patients to increased surgical time,
increased blood loss, and an increased risk of perioperative complications.
A grading system for osteotomies in the cervical spine was defined by Ames et al14 and
consists of the following:
Grades 1 and 2: facet joint resection
Grade 3: corpectomy
Grade 4: complete uncovertebral joint resection
Grades 5 and 6: opening and closing wedge osteotomies
Grade 7: complete vertebral column resection

Pitfalls and Preventive Measures
Anterior approach is associated with a risk of laryngeal nerve damage. The vocal cord
function of patients who have undergone previous anterior cervical spine surgery
should be assessed via laryngoscopy before undertaking a repeat anterior approach.
Severe cervical kyphosis may contribute to difficult intubation, in which case cervical
traction should be applied to facilitate the process. In extreme cases, tracheostomy
may be required preoperatively.
In performing an osteotomy at C7, a risk of durotomy and injury to the spinal cord
and C8 nerve roots exists.
Complications

Complications
The rates of complications and revision remain high in patients cervical spine deformity.
Studies have reported complication rates as high as 20% and revision rates as high as
12%.15-17 Complications associated with anterior and posterior approaches include
dysphagia, dysphonia, tracheal or esophageal injury, vertebral artery injury, cerebral
spinal fluid leak, wound complications, and implant failure.18 In addition, posterior
approaches may be complicated by temporary or permanent neurologic deficits.
Common reasons for revision include infection, adjacent segment degeneration,
postoperative junctional kyphosis, incomplete correction of deformity, and
pseudoarthrosis.
Distal Junctional Kyphosis

Distal Junctional Kyphosis
Distal junctional kyphosis (DJK) is a serious complication of corrective cervical spine
surgery and a common reason for revision surgery. Radiographs show DJK as a loss of
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:10 AM
AAOS | Adult Cervical Spine Deformity
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004088
15/19

alignment at the lowest instrumented vertebra or the lowest instrumented vertebra +2,
with a DJK angle greater than 10°. Risk factors for DJK include severe preoperative
cervical deformity as measured by cSVA, T1S–cervical lordosis, and thoracic kyphosis.16
Pseudarthrosis

Pseudarthrosis
Pseudarthrosis of the cervical spine is failure of fusion after a procedure intended to
create spinal arthrodesis. As many as 30% of patients may be asymptomatic, with the
condition detectable only on postoperative radiographs. Rates of pseudarthrosis are
particularly high after multilevel ACDF, and additional posterior fixation of the construct
may be necessary. Management of symptomatic pseudarthrosis often involves surgical
exploration and revision to achieve optimal arthrodesis and improved patient outcomes.
Outcomes

Outcomes
For cervical spine deformity, commonly used outcome measures include the Neck
Disability Index, the modified Japanese Orthopedic Association score, the Medical
Outcomes Study 36-Item Short Form, and the Scoliosis Research Society 22-Item
Questionnaire. These outcome measures quantify the effect of a cervical spine deformity
on a patients ability to perform activities of daily living, fulfill home and work
responsibilities, and maintain emotional and psychological health.
